headline: Jones Inlet runs blind as buoy feeds thin out heading into the June moon
subhead: With offshore stations offline and the SST package two days stale, bay thermal structure and bait position become the controlling read for the week.
body_markdown:
The honest lead today is what we don't have. The Dr. Fish analyst run came in with no live buoy temperatures in hand, the offshore triangle at 44017, 44039 and 44040 is dark, and the satellite SST package hasn't refreshed since June 8. That means the usual anchor for a Jones Inlet report — an ocean-side reading off the approaches paired with a bay number — has to be reconstructed from what the water was doing earlier in the week and what the bait and structure are telling us right now. The pattern through the first week of June was a classic early-summer split: bay water climbing faster than the ocean, a sharp thermal lip riding in and out of the inlet on each tide, and a southwest sea breeze rebuilding most afternoons. Nothing in the past 72 hours suggests that has broken down.

What that means for this beat is straightforward. The engine right now is the inlet itself — the temperature differential between Hempstead Bay water flushing out on the drop and cooler ocean water pushing back on the flood is doing all the work of concentrating bait. Fluke are the headline species, and the productive water is the deeper edges of the Sloop Channel sweep, the slope off the east side of the inlet down to the buoy line, and the cuts north and south of the Meadowbrook. This is squid-and-spearing season with a bucktail-and-Gulp dropper, and the slot-class fish — 17 to 19 inches — are stacked on the down-current side of the bridge abutments rather than out in the middle. Bass have shifted from the early-spring bunker-chase pattern to a more structure-locked night bite on the inlet rips and the Robert Moses pilings.

On the ground, the fluke bite inside the bay has been the most consistent thing going. The Meadowbrook southeast corner has had a fleet on it for weeks and there's a reason — the depth change combined with the bridge shadow holds bait through most of the incoming. The complaint I keep hearing, and that matches what the water is doing, is the wind ruining drifts when it clocks northeast or piles up against an incoming tide. When you get a clean southwest 8-to-12 with the incoming, the same drift produces twice the fish. Demo Point and the slope in front of Cedar Overlook have been picky but every drift puts a couple of 19-inchers in the boat, with a heavy sea bass bycatch on the north side of the Moses bridge that you can lean on if the flatties go quiet.

The back-bay blue and weakfish picture is improving in a way that matches the temperature curve. Snappers are already running 7 and 8 inches, which is ahead of schedule and tells you the bay warmed early and held. That same warm water is what's going to turn the weakfish bite on in the deeper holes off the Wantagh and around the channel edges south of Freeport — sundown into the first two hours of dark, small soft plastics on light jigheads, fished slow. Surf-side, Jones Beach and Short Beach have been quiet during daylight but the structure is set up for a clean night plug bite on the dropping tide, particularly along the west jetty inside corner where the current piles bait against the rocks.

Looking ahead three to five days, the controlling variable is the full moon on the 13th and the spring tides that come with it. Stronger flushing pulls more cold ocean water through the inlet on the flood, which will reset the thermal lip closer to the bridges and concentrate fluke tighter to structure rather than spreading them across open drifts. I'd be watching the Robert Moses bridges first thing on the outgoing the morning after the full moon — that's typically when the better-grade fluke move up onto the channel edges. If the offshore buoys come back online and we see ocean temps in the low 60s, expect the first real bluefish pushes through the inlet mouth on the outgoing, chasing bunker schools that have been sitting just off the beach.

Until the data pipeline catches up, read the bait. Birds working the inlet mouth on a dropping tide are telling you everything the buoys aren't, and the boats that have been putting fish in the cooler this past week are the ones fishing structure on the right side of the tide rather than running and gunning. That doesn't change with the moon.
